rationale: A wins because it gives the founder sharper proof gates, not just nicer angle labels. Its proof line asking what 'local-currency support' means — 'local BIN, local entity, local settlement, or FX at point of sale' — is the kind of question that prevents a launch pitch from blowing up in a reporter's hands. B is cleaner on grounding, but 'Brex's global card rollout is a bet that expense software has to go everywhere its customers do' stays more analyst-deck than reporter-ready.
gaps_in_A: 'multinational-payroll problem' drags payroll into a corporate-card and expense-management update. Cute headline, wrong aisle.
'Ramp can't copy quickly' is an unproved competitive claim. The set later admits it needs proof, but the headline already spent money it does not have.
'distributed hiring made every Series B a multi-country employer' invents a sweeping remote-work premise the update did not provide.
gaps_in_B: 'cards and local-currency reimbursement live in 50 countries at once, not a phased pilot' adds certainty the update does not explicitly give. The live-versus-rollout distinction needs verification before it becomes copy.
'horizontal software categories internationalize as their customer base globalizes' is consultant fog. It may be true, but it sounds like a conference panel until backed by examples.
'spends big on global infrastructure' infers cost and infrastructure scale from the launch. Reasonable suspicion, not a sourced fact.

The proof asks are solid but thinner than A's; 'confirmation of whether Ramp... already operates' is right, but it does not demand the country-by-country issuing versus reimbursement breakdown that will decide whether the 50-country claim survives contact with a reporter.
